message.content:
**Choosing the “best” ionisation method depends on what you’re trying to analyse, the sample matrix, the instrumentation, and the desired sensitivity/accuracy.** Below is a quick‑reference guide that compares the most common ionisation techniques used in mass spectrometry (MS) and highlights the scenarios where each shines. | Ionisation Technique | Principle | Typical MS Platforms | Strengths | Weaknesses | Best‑For | |----------------------|-----------|----------------------|-----------|------------|----------| | **Electron Impact (EI)** | High‑energy electrons (70 eV) knock out electrons from neutral molecules → hard ionisation → extensive fragmentation | GC‑MS | • Universal for volatile, thermally stable compounds
• Well‑characterised fragmentation libraries (NIST, Wiley)
• Robust, low‑maintenance | • Hard ionisation → little molecular ion for large/thermally labile species
• Requires volatile, non‑polar analytes | • Small, volatile organics (e.g., pesticides, VOCs) | | **Chemical Ionisation (CI)** | Reagent gas (CH₄, NH₃, H₂) ionised by electrons; reagent ions transfer charge to analyte → soft ionisation | GC‑MS | • Soft → often retains M⁺ or M⁺·
• Good for polar, thermally labile molecules | • Requires a suitable reagent gas
• Lower sensitivity than EI for some analytes | • Semi‑volatile, polar compounds (e.g., alcohols, esters) | | **Atmospheric Pressure Chemical Ionisation (APCI)** | Corona discharge ionises solvent vapour → protonated/deprotonated analytes | LC‑MS (mostly triple‑quadrupole, Q‑TOF) | • Soft, good for moderately polar, low‑MW compounds
• Handles high‑flow LC (up to 1 mL min⁻¹) | • Less effective for very polar or high‑MW molecules
• Requires a suitable solvent system | • Lipids, steroids, small drug metabolites | | **Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)** | Charged droplets formed by applying high voltage to liquid → solvent evaporates → ions released | LC‑MS (triple‑quad, Q‑TOF, Orbitrap) | • Very soft → preserves intact molecular ion
• Handles high‑MW, highly polar, ionic species
• Capable of tandem MS (MS/MS) | • Suppression by salts, high‑ionic‑strength matrices
• Requires aqueous or mixed solvents | • Peptides, proteins, nucleotides, complex metabolites | | **Matrix‑Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation (MALDI)** | Sample mixed with matrix, laser ablation → desorption/ionisation | MALDI‑TOF, MALDI‑TOF/TOF | • Ultra‑soft → intact ions for large biomolecules
• Fast, high‑throughput screening | • Matrix interference at low m/z
• Limited to analytes that can be co‑crystallised with matrix | • Proteins, peptides, oligonucleotides, polymers | | **Desorption Electrospray Ionisation (DESI)** | Ambient ionisation via charged solvent spray onto sample surface | Ambient MS (often coupled to GC‑MS or LC‑MS) | • No sample prep, real‑time analysis
• Works on solid surfaces | • Lower sensitivity than LC‑MS
• Limited to surface‑accessible analytes | • Forensic, pharmaceutical, food safety | | **Laser Ablation Electrospray Ionisation (LAESI)** | Laser ablation of tissue → plume mixed with electrospray → ionisation | Ambient MS | • Direct tissue analysis, minimal prep | • Requires laser‑ablation hardware | • Metabolomics, histology | | **Atmospheric Pressure Photoionisation (APPI)** | UV photons ionise solvent/analyte → charge transfer | LC‑MS | • Good for non‑polar, aromatic compounds
• Complementary to APCI | • Requires UV‑transparent solvents | • Polycyclic aromatics, PAHs | --- ### How to Pick the Right One 1. **Sample Polarity & Volatility** * Volatile, non‑polar → **EI** (GC‑MS). * Polar, semi‑volatile → **CI** (GC‑MS) or **APCI** (LC‑MS). * Highly polar, high‑MW → **ESI** (LC‑MS). 2. **Molecular Weight** * < 500 Da → EI, CI, APCI, ESI all work. * > 500 Da → ESI or MALDI (for biomolecules). 3. **Desired Fragmentation** * Need detailed fragmentation pattern → EI (libraries). * Want intact molecular ion → ESI, MALDI, APCI. 4. **Matrix Effects** * Complex biological matrices → ESI (with proper cleanup). * Solid surfaces → DESI, LAESI. 5. **Throughput & Sample Prep** * Rapid screening → DESI, MALDI. * Routine quantitative analysis → LC‑MS with ESI/APCI. --- ### Quick Decision Flow ``` ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Is the analyte volatile? ──► Yes → EI (GC‑MS) │ │ │ ▼ │ Is the analyte polar? ──► Yes → ESI (LC‑MS) or APCI (LC‑MS) │ │ │ ▼ │ Is the analyte large biomolecule? ──► Yes → MALDI (TOF) │ │ │ ▼ │ Default → ESI (LC‑MS) ``` --- ### Bottom Line - **For routine, high‑throughput screening of small, volatile organics:** **EI** on GC‑MS. - **For polar, thermally labile compounds in a liquid matrix:** **ESI** on LC‑MS. - **For large biomolecules (proteins, peptides):** **MALDI** or **ESI** (depending on the instrument). - **For non‑polar, high‑MW aromatics:** **APPI** or **APCI**. If you have a specific analyte class or application in mind, let me know and I can narrow it down further!
